## What is measured

The corpus is [PRL-PRG/r-benchmarks](https://github.com/PRL-PRG/r-benchmarks),
pinned to one commit, characterised in *What Do R Benchmarks Measure? Toward a
Performance-Characterized Benchmark Suite for R* (VMIL'26). Each program
defines `execute(size)` and, optionally, an untimed `setup()`. Timing,
repetition and process management belong to the shared harness, driven by the
[bench](https://github.com/PRL-PRG/bench) framework.

- **R's recommended packages** (MASS, Matrix, lattice, ...) are built with
  every release, as R's default build does: each R version runs with the
  versions it shipped with.
- Four benchmarks (`lr`, `lr_test`, `pca`, `pca-blocked`) also need
  clusterGeneration, used only to generate their input in `setup()`. Every
  build gets the version that was on CRAN at the date of its source; where it
  does not install, those benchmarks are recorded as unsupported.
- **Left out: `mathkernel/MMM-T1`.** Its time depends on where the linker
  places R's code (on one of eleven layouts it took 20% longer), so a run
  could not resolve a change smaller than about 10% in it; its kernel, a
  scalar triple loop over 200×200 matrices, is also `matmult_triplp`'s, which
  is among the steadiest benchmarks. The other 117 are measured.

## How R is built

- **Releases** are built from the CRAN source tarballs. **R-devel** (and
  R-patched) from the source snapshots CRAN publishes daily, which include the
  recommended packages, identified by their SVN revision.
- Every version is built **the way R builds by default**: a plain
  `./configure` (only the install prefix is given) and `make`. So R chooses
  its own flags (`-g -O2`), uses its internal BLAS and LAPACK, links into one
  `R` binary (no shared `libR`) and builds the recommended packages.
- **One compiler for every version:** GCC 16.2.0 as upstream builds it (the
  official `gcc:16` container image), in an image whose libraries come from a
  dated Ubuntu archive snapshot. A compiler change would move every number at
  once. Upstream GCC adds no hardening by itself (distributions' GCCs add
  `_FORTIFY_SOURCE`, stack protector, PIE and more), and its own `-O2`,
  vectoriser included, is used for every version.
- **Settings by version range.** A settings file adds compiler options to
  every version or to versions up to or from a given release. A source tree is
  placed by the version it declares, so a snapshot of R-devel gets the rules
  of the release it leads up to, and releases after R 4.6.2 keep the current
  settings.
- **The C dialect of the time.** Each version gets the default C dialect of
  the newest GCC released before it (gnu89 until GCC 4.9, gnu11 for GCC 5 to 7,
  gnu17 for GCC 8 to 14, gnu23 from GCC 15); R's `configure` then adds its own
  `-std` where it did at the time (`-std=gnu99` on top of gnu89, C23 from R
  4.5.0).
- **Settings that change no generated code** go to every version:
  `-fpermissive` (implicit declarations were warnings before GCC 14; without
  it R 3.0.0's `configure` silently decides `ftell` is broken),
  `-fallow-argument-mismatch` (Fortran, likewise before gfortran 10) and a
  `configure` answer that lets R before 4.2 accept curl 8. For R 4.6.2,
  `configure` decides exactly the same with and without them.
- **`-fcommon`** (the default before GCC 10) can change the generated code, so
  it goes only to the releases up to the newest one that does not link
  without it: R 3.6.1 and older (found by bisection; 3.6.2 links).
- R before 4.0 needs PCRE1, which Ubuntu no longer ships: it is built from
  its last release (8.45) with the same compiler.
- **Four code layouts of every build.** Where the linker places R's code
  moves some benchmarks' times by up to 20% (through branch prediction and the
  instruction cache), and any change to R moves the code. So every build is
  also linked three more times with 1000, 2100 and 3300 bytes of filler in
  front of R's own code (the first object after the C runtime's), placing it
  at four points spread over a 4 KiB page, the period of the instruction
  cache's sets, and not a whole number of KiB apart (four of the eleven
  layouts the run design was chosen on). Only the link
  is repeated: the binary is byte for byte what compiling with the filler
  gives, and the rest of the installation is the same files.

## How a run is measured

- Every benchmark runs in **4 separate R processes, one on each code
  layout**, each doing 1 warm-up and 4 measured iterations, as
  `R --slave --vanilla` under `setarch -R`. A run is four passes over the
  suite, one per layout, each in the same fixed shuffled order (about 75
  minutes for R 4.5.2).
- Before every iteration the harness collects garbage, then **idles for 1 ms**
  before starting the clock. Without the pause, the state one iteration left
  in the CPU's branch predictors carried into the next: about one
  `convolution` iteration in fifteen ran 37% slower, and `att3_5`, `em` and
  `matmult_triplp` moved by whole processes.
- Runs execute in the build's container, pinned to one isolated CPU core, with
  no network.
- The machine runs a pinned kernel, with the benchmark core isolated from the
  scheduler (`isolcpus`, `nohz_full`, `rcu_nocbs`), the performance governor,
  turbo off and the frequency fixed, address-space randomisation off
  system-wide, transparent huge pages off, and no power-management daemons. The
  batch system checks all of it before every job and refuses to run otherwise.
- **CPU temperature and thermal throttling** are sampled every second during
  every benchmark execution, which records its hottest reading and the throttle
  events counted during it. An execution during which the CPU came within
  10 °C of the limit the CPU itself declares, or throttled, is flagged as
  possibly affected.
- **A machine is a set of identical boxes** (same hardware, firmware settings
  and system): their results form one series, whichever box measured them.
  Before every run, two checks compare the box with its machine's reference,
  measured when the machine was calibrated:
  - the **probe**, a native program of the cluster, on the benchmark core
    after a warm-up: integer and branch throughput, cache and memory latency,
    memory bandwidth;
  - the **sentinel**, a few short benchmarks of the suite on a fixed build
    (R 4.5.2), after warm-up iterations.

  Within 3% of the reference the run is fine. Beyond it the run is still
  measured, but marked **suspect**: its results are shown with a warning and
  never used to detect changes. Beyond 10% (twice in a row for the probe) the
  box does not run benchmarks at all: it is taken out of service, and the job
  waits, held, until it is fixed.
- **A box runs a job only once fully booted:** systemd reports the boot
  complete, no start-up jobs are pending and it has been up for a minute (it
  is idle from about 30 s of uptime). Periodic maintenance (package updates, indexing, trims) is disabled on the
  boxes.

## Statistics

- A benchmark's time on a run is the **geometric mean over processes** of
  each process's median measured iteration. Its interval is a 95% t-interval
  on the log scale with the process as the unit of replication (3 degrees of
  freedom for one run, 6 for a comparison of two). Each run's standard error
  has a **floor of 0.1%** added: what a run carries beyond the spread of its
  processes. A comparison therefore never resolves a change below about 0.35%.
- A **speedup** is *time(A) / time(B)*: above 1× means B is faster. Speedups
  are only ever computed between runs on the **same machine** and under the
  **same methodology version**.
- The **baseline** (1×) is the R version shipped in the **newest Ubuntu LTS**,
  currently R `r BASELINE_VERSION` in Ubuntu `r UBUNTU_LTS$ubuntu[nrow(UBUNTU_LTS)]`:
  the R most Linux users get without adding CRAN's repository. The table of
  which R each LTS ships (`r paste0(UBUNTU_LTS$r, " in ", UBUNTU_LTS$ubuntu, collapse = ", ")`)
  is kept in `data/ubuntu-lts.csv`. Every build checks Ubuntu's release list
  for a newer LTS and reads the `r-base` version it shipped from Launchpad, so
  when a new LTS is released every speedup on the site is **rescaled to its R**
  at the next build. A machine that has not measured that release uses its oldest
  measured release instead.
- Suite-level numbers are **geometric means** over the benchmarks that every
  compared run could execute. The count is always shown, because old releases
  cannot run benchmarks that need newer R.
- R-devel **change detection** flags a benchmark when it moves by more than
  2% and outside its interval relative to the previous seven good nights, and
  the next three nights confirm it.

## How the run design was chosen

On the kabylake machine, R 4.5.2 was measured on eleven code layouts and then
under this design six times, each run on four of the layouts. Comparing every
two of those runs (the same build, so no change to find), with the 117
benchmarks:

- an interval excluded no change in 2.1% of the comparisons (95% intervals
  allow 5%), and **no benchmark was flagged** (a change above 2% outside its
  interval) in any of them;
- a comparison of two runs resolves a change of **0.43%** for the median
  benchmark, 1.2% at the 90th percentile; 16 benchmarks above 1%, 3 above 2%
  (`heat`, `rw2d1` and `pidigits`, whose layouts or processes vary most);
- for all but a few benchmarks, runs differed no more than the spread of
  their processes predicts; the largest excess, in `reversecomplement` and
  `pidigits`, was 0.6–0.7%, well below the 2% a change must exceed to be
  flagged.

The first iteration of a process is slower for most benchmarks (by 1.9% at
the median, up to 39%); from the second on, iterations differ from the steady
state no more than from each other, so one warm-up is enough.

## Profiles {#profiles}

A second pass, a job of its own, records each benchmark 5 times with
`perf record --call-graph dwarf,32768` at 999 Hz, user-space cycles only,
on the same build: R as built (the first code layout), on the same isolated
core, never in the timing pass. Each recording is one R process that runs
`setup()` and then `execute()` once. Only samples inside `execute()` are kept,
using phase markers the harness prints. Each sample
is charged to the **innermost stack frame** a rule recognises, checked in this
order:

1. **Object rules:** frames in BLAS/LAPACK libraries are `native-blas`, and
   frames in a package's own shared object are `native-ffi`.
2. **Symbol rules:** a table of named interpreter functions (for example
   `bcEval` → interpreter, `R_findVar` → lookup, `Rf_duplicate` →
   mem-duplicate).
3. **Shape rule:** `do_*` and `ALT*` functions inside the interpreter are
   `primitives`, apart from the dispatch primitives (`UseMethod`,
   `NextMethod`, `standardGeneric`).

Samples no rule reaches are reported as **unattributed** and never hidden;
samples whose innermost recognised frame is R's main loop are `other`. A
benchmark's share of a category is the mean over its recordings. A profile
run whose mean unattributed share exceeds 5% fails the quality gate and is
not published. The rules were
validated (VMIL'26) on builds like these, without frame pointers. Profiles on platforms without `perf` (macOS:
samply) are marked *experimental* until their category shares are shown to
agree with perf.
